claims.text: The laws are named for Augustus De Morgan, whose Formal Logic: or, The Calculus of Inference, Necessary and Probable was published in London in 1847 — the same year as Boole’s first book on symbolic logic, the two men being correspondents.

source.title: De Morgan, A., Formal Logic: or, The Calculus of Inference, Necessary and Probable, Taylor and Walton, London, 1847

claims.text: The laws state that the negation of a conjunction is the disjunction of the negations, and the negation of a disjunction is the conjunction of the negations: not (A and B) is equivalent to (not A) or (not B), and not (A or B) is equivalent to (not A) and (not B).

source.title: De Morgan, A., Formal Logic: or, The Calculus of Inference, Necessary and Probable, Taylor and Walton, London, 1847

claims.text: Boole argued in An Investigation of the Laws of Thought, 1854, that three operations — conjunction, disjunction and negation — suffice to perform all logical functions.

source.title: Boole, G., An Investigation of the Laws of Thought, on Which are Founded the Mathematical Theories of Logic and Probabilities, Walton and Maberly, London, 1854

claims.text: In older circuit-engineering notation, where complement is written as an apostrophe or an overbar, the laws appear as (AB)′ = A′ + B′ — a form that comes from Shannon’s application of the algebra to switching circuits.

source.title: Shannon, C. E., A Symbolic Analysis of Relay and Switching Circuits, MIT master’s thesis 1937; Transactions of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers 57:713-723, 1938

beats.broke: negating a compound condition requires reasoning about what the whole thing means, and that reasoning is where people make the mistake
beats.fix: two rewriting rules that push a negation inwards mechanically — flip the connective, negate both sides — with no understanding required
beats.cost: the rewrite is valid about truth values and says nothing about evaluation order or side effects, which is where it stops being safe in a program
beats.interview: why a mechanical rule beats understanding the condition
